items.title: xdsclient: flush any unsent loads when the LRS stream is closed

labels.name: Area: xDS
labels.description: Includes everything xDS related, including LB policies used with xDS.

items.body:
The LRS implementation in the xDS client transport can be found here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L47

The `ReportLoad()` API returns a cancel func which is plumbed all the way to the user of the `XDSClient` API here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/client.go#L56

The current implementation of this cancel function simply cancels the context passed to the LRS stream, which results in the stream getting closed. But what we really want is for unsent loads to be flushed on the stream before it is closed.

The xDS client transport spawns the `lrsRunner` goroutine https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L95 which (in a backoff loop) sends the first LRS request, receives the first response and then calls `sendLoads` to periodically send out load reports https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/55d8783479c7cc1a72a435340432702a67d809aa/xds/internal/xdsclient/transport/loadreport.go#L153

What we want is for the cancel function to synchronize with `sendLoads` so that when the cancel function is invoked, it results in unsent loads being flushed before the stream context is cancelled.

items.body:
👋 Hey there! I've spent a bit too much time mulling over docs and Github issues trying to understand the retry logic provided here, so I figure I'll just ask for clarification!

To provide some context, I was initially attempting to avoid implementing my own retry logic, and was inspired by [this example](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/master/examples/features/retry/README.md) to configure service config for retries. On doing so, I became a bit confused by the configuration. By tearing down my gRPC server and standing it back up again, I was able to see that the client connection was being re-established, but what confused me was that there was no point where the retries seemed to "give up". Given the maxAttempts value in the example, I would think that the retries would "give up" pretty quickly, but I found that it seemed to retry indefinitely. I could also confirm that the longer I waited, the longer it would take for the connection to be re-established when I started the server again, which seems to indicate the exponential backoff is coming into play.

After some digging around, I think the issue in my case was that the server config retries only seem to cater to RPC calls that are explicitly met with status codes from the server. I was very confused because the client errors I was receiving had the UNAVAILABLE status code, which I was configuring the retryPolicy for, but I imagine the policy doesn't come into play unless that code is provided via the server rather than via the client / library. Is that accurate?

I'm left a bit confused because, if the above is true, I would think that the retryPolicy I set before wasn't doing anything, but I could confirm that the library was retrying internally as opposed to returning errors, so I'm not quite sure what was changed.

I then came across the [backoff package](https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/grpc/backoff) and [connection backoff protocol](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/connection-backoff.md). Given my server was down altogether, this seemed promising and that it was more of a connection backoff that I wanted. After configuring this with ConnectParams when dialing, it didn't seem as though this was doing anything, as (while my server was down) dialing was continuing to return errors and didn't seem to be attempting to retry at all.

I should mention that, due to my server being down as I test, the error I receive is a "connection refused" error, and I recall reading somewhere that only temporary connection issues qualify for retry. Is that accurate?


So, to summarize my questions:
- If configuring retries via service config, do the RetryableStatusCodes fields need to be returned via server rather than client / library? i.e. is an UNAVAILABLE error due to "connection refused" not applicable?
- If enabling retries via service config retryPolicy, what happens to connection-style errors? It seems those changed when the retryPolicy was enabled.
- How do I opt into the connection backoff protocol? Is it enabled by default? Does enabling the service config retryPolicy enable it?
- Why does the connection backoff protocol not seem to be applying? Is it not relevant for "connection refused" errors?
- Am I chasing a dead end looking for retry logic that covers all connection-style errors? Must this be implemented manually? Is there any recommended best-practice here?

Ultimately, I'm hoping to maintain indefinite server-streams that will reconnect on the client should the server go away for any reason and continue to attempt to reconnect until the server returns.

Thanks!

items.title: rls: update picker synchronously upon receipt of configuration update
items.body:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/5469 recommends an audit of existing LB policies to ensure that they update their pickers synchronously upon receipt of a configuration update.

`rls` LB policy does not update its picker synchronously in one corner case.

- Configuration updates are handled here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L252
- The LB policy inhibits picker updates until the new configuration is pushed to all child policies. See: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L270
- In a blocking fashion, it does the following
  - pushes updates to child policies
  - waits for picker updates from all the child policies
  - sends a new picker
  - See: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L293
- At the end of `UpdateClientConnState`, the LB policy handles any changes to the data cache size here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L297
  - The return value from the resize operation is ignored here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/b4f7947184ed45e72283a37aeaf214e38c35bc63/balancer/rls/balancer.go#L306
  - The return value should not be ignored. Instead if any entry with a backoff timer was evicted, then it should result in a new picker being sent upwards.

Quoting this from the design:
```
When removing an entry whose backoff_time_ is in the future, the backoff timer 
will be cancelled.  Note that just like when the backoff timer fires normally, a new
 picker is returned to the channel, to force it to re-process any wait-for-ready RPCs
that may still be queued if we failed them while we were in backoff.
```

items.title: pickfirst: Use one subConn per address

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

labels.name: Type: Behavior Change
labels.description: Behavior changes not categorized as bugs

items.body:
As part of the [Dual Stack implementation](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A61-IPv4-IPv6-dualstack-backends.md#java-and-go-pick-first-restructuring), we would like to move the pickfirst algorithm out of the subConn and in the lb policy

>We would like to take this opportunity to move toward a more uniform cross-language architecture. Also, moving pick_first up to the LB policy layer in Java and Go will have the nice effect of making their backoff work per-address instead of across all addresses, which is what C-core does and what the (poorly specified) [connection backoff spec](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/connection-backoff.md) seems to have originally envisioned.

This change moves the algorithm into the lb policy and ensures the LB creates one subConn per address, but doesn't remove the the pickfirst logic from the subConn. Happy eyeballs is not implemented.

Inspiration is taken from the c-core implementation:
* latest: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/src/core/load_balancing/pick_first/pick_first.cc
* before happy eyeballs: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/b6f01c6/src/core/ext/filters/client_channel/lb_policy/pick_first/pick_first.cc

## Other changes
* Add an `ExitIdle()` method on `stateRecordingBalancer`. This is required as [the fallback logic of re-connecting all the subConns](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/4e9b5968af1aeffb0cb44e772aa69a4b4e44a722/internal/balancer/gracefulswitch/gracefulswitch.go#L229-L233) no longer works. This is because the LB policy closes the active subConn once the connection is dropped and does a pick first over all the addresses when `ExitIdle` is called. When all the subConns are shutdown, re-connecting will have no effect.
* Update tests with new assertions based on the new behaviour.

## Behaviour Changes
* Pickfirst now creates one subchannel per address.
* An exponential back-off is performed per server address when the subchannel enters transient failure.
* After every address has been tried one, pickfirst attempts to re-connect to the addresses in the order in which they complete their back-off, this is not deterministic.

RELEASE NOTES:
* Pickfirst creates one subchannel per address.

items.title: ring_hash stuck in TransientFailure despite having available endpoints
items.body:
### What version of gRPC are you using?

This most likely affects all version since ring hash behavior to always attempt to connect to at least one endpoint was added via https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/5338.

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?

go version go1.22.4 darwin/arm64

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?

MacOS 14.5

### What did you do?

Use the `ring_hash` balancer with 2 priorities:
- The highest priority has 3+ endpoints, and none is available
- The lower priority has at least one available endpoint.

### What did you expect to see?

If some of the endpoints in the highest priority becomes available, but not all of them (technically, at least 2 are still not available), the traffic should go back to the endpoints with highest priority.

### What did you see instead?

The traffic _sometimes_ continues to go to the lower priority indefinitely, until the endpoints change.

### Additional notes

The ring hash balancer is specifically designed to avoid that situation, as outlines in [A42: xDS Ring Hash LB Policy - Aggregated Connectivity States](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A42-xds-ring-hash-lb-policy.md#aggregated-connectivity-state):

> In addition, once the `ring_hash` policy reports `TRANSIENT_FAILURE`, it needs some way to recover from that state.  The `ring_hash` policy normally requires pick requests to trigger subchannel connection attempts, but if it is being used as a child of the `priority` policy, it will not be getting any picks once it reports `TRANSIENT_FAILURE`. To work around this, it will make sure that it is attempting to connect (after applicable backoff period) to at least one subchannel at any given time.  After a given subchannel fails a connection attempt, it will move on to the next subchannel in the ring.  It will keep doing this until one of the subchannels successfully connects, at which point it will report `READY` and stop proactively trying to connect.

I believe that the solution implementated in Go in https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/pull/5338 is not complete. Specifically, it always walks the ring *from the start* forward looking for an endpoint that is not the endpoint we are currently trying to connect to. As a result, if the ring contains an endpoint twice *before* every endpoints (i.e. the ring looks like `[A B A C]` rather than `[A B C A]`, which is very likely), it will cycle through the list of endpoints at the beginning of the ring until the duplicate (in this case `[A B]`), without trying the remaining endpoints (`C`).

items.title: pickfirst: improve behavior when the first address is a blackhole

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
With the current implementation, if the `pick_first` LB policy is given a set of addresses where the first address is a blackhole i.e the connection just hangs and does not fail before the connection timeout expires, the LB policy employs an exponential backoff mechanism and retries the connection attempt. But when it retries, it again starts from the first address. This means that when the first address is a blackhole, the other addresses never get a chance.

To improve the behavior in this scenario, we could try doing one of the following:
- when retrying, the `pick_first` LB policy could start from where it left off in the address list, instead of starting from the top
- instead of creating one `SubConn` with all addresses in it and letting the channel implement the logic of using the first good address, change the `pick_first` LB policy to create one `SubConn` for each address and apply the connection timeout and backoff for each `SubConn` separately.

Option #2 is more work, but might be the better way to go.

items.title: Hang on connection, same timeout for connection and RPC?
Client waits with DNS query when no channel's available
items.body:
### What version of gRPC are you using?
v1.61.0

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
1.21.7

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?
Linux

### What did you do?

In production we're using a Kubernetes statefulset for the servers and a deployment for the client. Let's assume the replica count for the servers is two (`server-0` and `server-1`). We're using a headless service on top of the statefulset:
```
NAME     TYPE        CLUSTER-IP   EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
server   ClusterIP   None         <none>        9090/TCP,8080/TCP
```
On the client the server address is configured as `dns:///server.default:9090` and round robin load balancing is enabled by
``` go
grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(`{"loadBalancingPolicy":"round_robin"}`)
```
This setup works nicely to distribute the load evenly among the statefulset pods.

The issue is when we try to rolling upgrade the statefulset:
1. Kubernetes terminates `server-1`, which calls `GracefulStop` and disconnects the client.
2. A new `server-1` pod is started, with a different IP address.
3. The service endpoint is immediately updated with the new IP address.
4. Kubernetes terminates `server-0`.

### What did you expect to see?

At this point the endpoints for the service are the two new IP addresses for the server instances. We expect the client to use these addresses. We expect the grpc go client to immediately send a DNS query to get the new IP addresses for the `server.default` domain name.

### What did you see instead?

All RPCs in the client return with errors similar to this:
``` 
rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = last connection error: connection error: 
desc = "transport: error while dialing: dial tcp A.B.C.D:9090: connect: connection refused"
```
where A.B.C.D is the IP address of one of the old server pods.

Running a tcpdump with `port 53` on the client pod reveals that the grpc client does not send a DNS query for a long time after none of the old addresses are available. This "long" time is not always exactly the same, we measured anywhere between 30 seconds and 2 minutes.

### Alternatives considered

- First, we checked if the operating system caches the DNS entries, but that's not the case. We could always see the DNS query in tcpdump when manually resolving the server address.
- We tried to delay the rolling update (wait between the pod restarts), but that didn't solve the issue. From the moment only the new pod IPs are available, the issue stands. Moreover, delaying the deployment has other downsides.
- Adding sufficiently long (more than 2 minutes) retries to the client changes the issue from erroring out to being extremely slow, but obviously this is not a good solution.

I read through a lot of issues but couldn't find a solution for this. There is an [open grpc issue](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/12295) but without a solution.

items.title: Wait for ready with "readiness timeout"

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
### Use case(s) - what problem will this feature solve?

We have a long running stream (`rpc Stream(StreamRequest) returns (stream StreamResponse) {}`). On the client side we would like to open the stream and then have it open indefinitely. If a recoverable error happens, we would like to restart it. If a non-recoverable error happens, we would like to quit. 

### Proposed Solution

It would be great if the WaitForReady flag had an optional "readiness timeout": a timeout only for having the connection ready, not for the whole RPC.

### Alternatives Considered

#### Timeout in the retry config
``` json
{
  "methodConfig": [{
    "name": [{"service": "..."}],
    "waitForReady": true,
    "timeout": "10s",
  }]
}
```
The timeout in the above config unfortunately stops the stream even if it's ready (and flowing).

#### Stream context timeout
``` go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3 * time.Second)
defer cancel()
stream, err := client.Stream(ctx, &streampb.StreamRequest{})
```
Same issue: this will cancel the stream after 3 seconds even if there were no errors at all.

#### Connection context timeout
``` go
// waitForReady is true in the retryConfig
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3 * time.Second)
defer cancel()
conn, err := grpc.DialContext(ctx, address, grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(retryConfig))
```
This will never timeout if the server is not available.

#### Timeout in a different goroutine
``` go
timeout := 3 * time.Second
timer := time.NewTimer(timeout)
errCh := make(chan error)
go func() {
  stream, err := client.Stream(ctx, &streampb.StreamRequest{})
  defer timer.Stop()
  if err != nil {
    errCh <- err
    return
  }
  errCh <- readStream(ctx, stream)
}()
go func() {
  <-timer.C
  errCh <- fmt.Errorf("stream timeout after %s", timeout)
}()
return <-errCh
```
This works as expected: if we manage to connect to the stream within 3 seconds, it will stream until `ctx` is canceled. If we don't, we return an error. The problem is that the error is not very helpful ("stream timeout after 3s"). We cannot use the stream returned by `client.Stream()`, because with wait for ready it never returns.

items.title: rls: response with no targets should be treated as an error
items.body:
According to the original design:
```
An RLS request is considered to have succeeded if it returns an OK status and the 
RLS response's targets list contains at least one non-empty entry.
```

We are currently handling the case of a response with zero targets the same way we would handle a successful response. This means that when an RPC is made, the cache entry will not have any READY child policy wrappers, and hence will be queued until the RPC context expires. Instead, we should treat this case as an error and set the cache entry in backoff. The code that handles an RLS response is here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/32e3ef1ed1c494e3d748b93d67a0b7ec5d089a49/balancer/rls/picker.go#L216

items.title: xdsclient: Comply with A57 (failure modes)
items.body:
[A57](https://github.com/markdroth/proposal/blob/xds_client_behavior/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md) describes the expected behavior of the xDS client under different failure modes.

- [ADS Stream Termination](https://github.com/markdroth/proposal/blob/xds_client_behavior/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md#handling-ads-stream-termination)
  - According to the gRFC, only ADS stream failures which happen without ever having received a response from the server are to be considered as connection errors. In this case, the xDS client is supposed to log the error and report the same error to all watchers.
    - Our current implementation throws a `Warning` log. This should be changed to `Error` log. This can have some implications related to the test logger used in our tests which fails the test if it sees any logs thrown at error severity. We might have to add this error log to the list of acceptable errors, where applicable.
    - Our current implementation throws the log and informs all watchers, even in the case where a response from the server was received. This needs fixing to comply with A57.
    - Our backoff implementation upon ADS stream failures is already A57 compliant.
- [Connectivity Failure](https://github.com/markdroth/proposal/blob/xds_client_behavior/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md#handling-connectivity-failure)
  - We fall into the [bucket of implementations](https://github.com/markdroth/proposal/blob/xds_client_behavior/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md#connectivity-status-information-via-ads-stream-failure) which rely on ADS stream failures to detect connectivity failures.
    - We currently set `WaitForReady` on the ADS stream. This needs fixing to be A57 compliant.
- [Resource does not exist](https://github.com/markdroth/proposal/blob/xds_client_behavior/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md#handling-resources-that-do-not-exist)
  - This section might be the one which might need bigger changes for compliance with A57.
  - A57 specifies when the resource timer should start.
    - We currently start it the first time a watch is being registered for a resource. We do not consider the connectivity state of the channel in this scenario. A57 wants us to do that.
    - Also, A57 wants us to start a fresh timer after every stream restart if the associated resource was never received from the server in the past.
    - Both these requirements mean that it is much easier to take care of this timer at the transport layer rather than at the `authority` layer (this is the case after the refactor for generic API) or the `pubsub` layer (this is current implementation).
    
@dfawley 
I propose that we take care of these changes after the generic API changes are done. Especially #3 since it seems to be more involved.

items.body:
The xdsclient needed some modification to align to the Failure Mode Behavior specified in [A57](https://github.com/grpc/proposal/blob/master/A57-xds-client-failure-mode-behavior.md). This diff adds the following changes: 

1. Per A57, gRPC-Go should not use `wait_for_ready` while creating the ADS stream. This is because we depend on the stream to fail when the channel is in `TRANSIENT_FAILURE`, in order to obtain the status message for the connectivity failure.

1. Previously, the timer to watch resource was initialized when authority.watchResource() api was called. 

    Per A57
    > The timeout period should start as soon as both of the following are true:
    > 
    > The first message subscribing to the resource has been sent on the stream.
    > A connection has been established to the xDS server and the stream has been dispatched to the associated transport.
  
     In this change, the timer starts only when the transport signals back to the authority after a successful send().

1. A new resource watch state `watchStateRespRequested` to represent when the resource request has been sent by the transport
1. Add `OnSendHandler` to transport.Options to send updates from transport.

Fixes: #5753

* xdsclient/transport: stop using wait_for_ready dial option when creating ads stream + xdsclient/authority: watch resource timer starts after transport sends resource request

items.body:
This PR is a full-fledged refactor of the transport layer implementation of the xdsclient. It does not touch the existing implementation, and therefore existing implementation will be used until subsequent refactors which will involve the authority/controller/pubsub components.

Summary of changes:
- New transport implementation in `xds/internal/xdsclient/transport` which supports only xDS v3 transport protocol. We are getting rid of v2 support. So, it does not make sense to add v2 support here. 
  - Existing implementation is found in `xds/internal/xdsclient/controller/`.
- New implementation strictly deals only with transport protocol functionality.
  - It exposes an API to send requests for xDS resources. Existing implementation exposes a watch style API. A watch should be a higher layer abstraction and not a transport layer one.
  - The API to send requests needs to contain all the resources to be requested. Transport layer still needs to keep track of the resources being requested because it needs to re-request them upon stream failure.
  - Load reporting API is changed to not accept a server parameter. This is as per federation design. Each transport instance is supposed to talk to *one* management server for both ADS and LRS.
- New Transport API has the following key details
  - Accepts a function to report received resources. This function will be implemented by the data model layer to validate the received resources. The `authority` layer will also keep track of what resources it requested and will cache the received resources.
  - Accepts a function to report stream failures. This is used to propagate stream failures up to the resource watchers at the `authority` layer.
- Tests are in the same directory but in a different package, to ensure that they rely only on functionality and not internal details/state.

This refactor ensures that the transport layer has the following properties:
- Has very few dependencies on other parts of the xdsClient.
- Does not look into the resources. That will be the duty of the data model layer.

#resource-agnostic-xdsclient-api

items.title: rls: suppress picker updates from children when handling config updates

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
Summary of changes:
- Use a single channel to process the different events handled by the `run()` goroutine.
- Handling config updates from parent: `UpdateClientConnState()`
  - Handles config updates inline instead of pushing them on to a channel.
  - Sets a flag to inhibit picker updates.
  - After handling the config changes and pushing the required configs to child policies, queues an event to resume picker updates.
  - Waits for the above event to be acted upon, and then returns a new picker.
- Handling state updates from child: `UpdateState()`
  - Handled asynchronously as before. The only change is that message is pushed on the single channel used by `run()` goroutine.
- Pushing picker updates to the parent: `SendNewPickerLocked()`
  - If picker updates are inhibited (by the flag set in `UpdateClientConnState`), a new picker is built but is not pushed up.

What these change means is that when the RLS LB policy is handling a config update from its parent, no picker updates will be pushed up. This includes picker updates caused by events such as RLS response, cache timer expiry, backoff timer expiry etc.

Fixes https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/5211

Hi, 

I'm trying to catch as many connection errors as possible when dialing from grpc client to grpc server. I am already using the `grpc.WithReturnConnectionError()` dial option to get the latest connection error. This doesn't help for me, because I am using a **clustered** grpc server and I need more than the latest error, because this will only return the error of the last cluster node. And even if the grpc client successfully connects to a cluster node, I want to know, if any of the previous connection establishments failed.

I am aware of the `GRPC_GO_LOG_VERBOSITY_LEVEL=99` and `GRPC_GO_LOG_SEVERITY_LEVEL=info` environment variables, but I want to build a custom error management.

I am also aware of the `grpc.WithContextDialer(...)` dial option, but this only helps to detect DNS and TCP issues, not TLS. And even with a custom `grpc.WithTransportCredentials(...)` I was not able to catch 100% of possible dial errors.

### Proposed Solution

There is already a function `func (cc *ClientConn) updateConnectionError(err error) {...}` that stores the latest connection error. This function could be extended with an optional callback that will be called on connection errors. The callback could then be passed as dial option, e.g. `grpc.WithOnConnectionError(func(addr resolver.Address, err error) {...})`.

In #5238, we made a change to apply the default service config when grpc receives invalid service config from the name resolver (and a default service config exists).

If the client has not previously selected a valid service config or no service config,
for example a new client, then it treats the resolution attempt as having failed
(e.g., for a polling-based resolver, it should retry the query after appropriate backoff).
In other words, the channel will remain in state TRANSIENT_FAILURE until the

This PR does the following:
- undoes some of the changes from #5238, by not applying the default service config
- Renames `test/resolver_test.go` to `test/config_selector_test.go`  (since it contained only config selector related tests)

items.title: grpc lb health no time interval, so my cpu is red
Connection age context

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
### Use case(s) - what problem will this feature solve?

I have a server that handles long running bi-directional streams. Clients establishes a connection and then server may eventually have something to reply with. The request may be open for minutes, hours, days. In the middle there is a load balancer so I have to ensure the connection is closed before the timeout setting on the load balancer, otherwise it aborts the connection. To do that server has max connection age set to a number and in addition to that on each request code starts a timing out context. Once it times out, the server just returns `nil` from the handler, closing the connection cleanly. Client sees `io.EOF` and reconnects immediatelly, likely using a different TCP connection.

The problem is that sometimes the server has multiple things to reply with over a period of time that is smaller than max connection age. In this case the underlying TCP connection is reused and my timeout context only signals "done" when it's too late and the max connection age grace has also expired. Actually, the request's context signals sooner than my own context. The client gets an error (`rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = closing transport due to: connection error: desc = "error reading from server: EOF", received prior goaway: code: NO_ERROR, debug data:`) rather than `io.EOF`.

### Proposed Solution

Let the request handler know how much time it can occupy the connection for without breaching the max connection age. Ideally it's a context that is canceled when max connection age duration elapses.

Request context is a different thing. It's "done" when max connection age grace duration elapses and the connection is aborted. Even if handler returns `nil`, client gets an error.

### Alternatives Considered

For now I have came up with a workaround - max poll duration that a handler can wait for an event is just a little under 50% of the max connection age. And then max connection age for gRPC is set to 35% of the max connection age for the load balancer. This way even if some time is "consumed" by the "fast" requests, a long request that starts right before 
max connection age for gRPC expires, can still run for ~50% of time and end without breaching the overall max connection age of the load balancer. 35% is because it's 35% +/- 10% jitter - must be under 50%.

The above works but it's wasteful as connections could be sitting idle for much longer. Instead, both server and client have to do work to re-establish the network and logic connection/etc.

### Additional Context

Fix/workaround is here https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/cluster-integration/gitlab-agent/-/merge_requests/424, perhaps it can help understand the issue I'm having. Thank you.

items.title: Re-resolution loop when service config is not supported
items.body:
### What version of gRPC are you using?

v1.25.0 or later

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?

`go version go1.13.4 darwin/amd64`

### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version?

Mac, Linux

### What did you do?
If possible, provide a recipe for reproducing the error.

### What did you expect to see?

For DNS resolver, the default frequency of DNS resolution is 30 minutes, so DNS resolution happens every 30 minutes.

### What did you see instead?

For DNS resolver, the minimum duration for re-resolution is set to 30 seconds by `minDNSResRate`. When Service Config is invalid, DNS resolution happens every 30 seconds. This happens even if service config feature is not used, which means txt lookup returns error.

This is because of [polling](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/v1.25.x/resolver_conn_wrapper.go#L221-L231) that is introduced from v1.25.0 for error handling. The `NewServiceConfig` is called from resolver when service config is updated. 
In DNS resolver, [watcher](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/blob/v1.25.x/internal/resolver/dns/dns_resolver.go#L267) calls NewServiceConfig. The polling calls `ResolveNow` to do immediate re-resolution, so the request of dns resolution is queued in dns resolver. The request also makes a call of `NewServiceConfig`, so it becomes infinite loop.

If a resolver calls NewServiceConfig as a result of ResolveNow, the resolver possibly becomes loops. I'm not sure which part is bad, but NewServiceConfig should not be called when service config is disabled and it is better to have backoff for re-resolution.

items.title: Implement new requirement of completing protocol handshaking before 'READY'

labels.name: Type: Behavior Change
labels.description: Behavior changes not categorized as bugs

items.body:
**Detailed description of upcoming changes**:

gRPC-Go clients currently (in the 1.17 release and earlier) do not wait for the HTTP/2 handshake to complete before considering a connection ready for sending RPCs.  However, the client does not consider the connection to be "successful" unless the server's handshake is received before a connection error occurs.  An "unsuccessful" connection results in a backoff being performed before redialing.

This behavior will be changed during development for the 1.18 release.  The new default behavior will be to wait for the server handshake before considering the connection ready for sending RPCs.  This behavior can be tested in 1.17 by setting the environment variable `GRPC_GO_REQUIRE_HANDSHAKE=on`.  (This is the current behavior of gRPC-Java.)

Setting the environment variable to "`off`" will cause gRPC-Go clients to not wait for the handshake before considering the connection ready.  However, if a connection error occurs, backoff will not be performed and the client will attempt to connect to the first address returned by the name resolver.  This can lead to DOS problems and is not recommended.  (This is the current behavior of gRPC-C and was the behavior of gRPC-Go ~1 yr ago before #1648.)

During development for the 1.19 release, support for changing this behavior via the environment variable will be removed entirely.  Also, the `grpc.WithWaitForHandshake()` `DialOption` (was "experimental"; now "deprecated") will be removed.

**Users impacted**: as far as we are aware, the only usage that may be impacted by the new behavior is cmux.  cmux has [a workaround for Java](https://github.com/soheilhy/cmux#limitations) using `MatchWithWriters` to allow it to continue working in the face of this behavior.

For more information, see: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/17006

> When security is disabled, not waiting for the HTTP/2 handshake can lead to DoS-style behavior. For details, see: grpc/grpc-go#954. This requirement will incur an extra half-RTT latency before the first RPC can be sent under plaintext, but this is negligible and unencrypted connections are rarer than secure ones.
>
> Under TLS, the server will effectively send its part of the HTTP/2 handshake along with its final TLS "server finished" message, which the client must wait for before transmitting any data securely. This means virtually no extra latency is incurred by this requirement.
>
> Go had attempted to separate "connection ready" with "connection successful" (Issue: grpc/grpc-go#1444 PR: grpc/grpc-go#1648). However, this is confusing to users and introduces an arbitrary distinction between these two events. It has led to several bugs in our reconnection logic (e.g.s grpc/grpc-go#2380, grpc/grpc-go#2391, grpc/grpc-go#2392), due to the complexity, and it makes custom transports (grpc/proposal#103) more difficult for users to implement.
>
> We are aware of some use cases (in particular, soheilhy/cmux) expecting the behavior of transmitting an RPC before the HTTP/2 handshake is completed. Before making behavior changes to implement this, we will reach out to our users to the best of our abilities.

items.title: grpc-go server becomes unresponsive after Layer-3 congestion event
items.body: ### What version of gRPC are you using? 1.15 ### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)? 1.12 ### What operating system (Linux, Windows, …) and version? Debian Linux (stretch-slim, kernel 4.15.0) ### What did you do? This is a bizarre bug. My company operates many of its own networks and data centers. On one occasion we observed our gRPC services become unresponsive after a network congestion event and did not recover. There are many components in our networks. We are running an on-prem deployment of a few gRPC services in Kubernetes. We have clients in another VLAN connected to a switch that routes connections to another VLAN in our data center with a F5 load balancer in front of it. This data center houses our Kubernetes cluster and has an NGINX ingress controller with the grpc module enabled for routing all HTTP/2 traffic to a ClusterIP service backed by pods running the grpc-go application containers described herein. To summarize, here is the full path of all the unary and streaming RPCs along the connections that are established between all the hops described above. ``` clients <=> IRB VLAN switch <=> F5 load balancer <=> nginx-ingress <=> k8s service <=> pods ``` With the above details in mind, below is the full sequence of events. The network has clients that are physically connected to a switch with IRB for routing and bridging between VLANs. Around 11:15 am one day we observed a brief spike in Layer-3 traffic on this switch effectively maxing out a 1 Gbps interface for a few minutes: ![1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1788878/61925373-e35f5200-af20-11e9-9425-4d87e5c87964.png) As this was happening and as traffic on the switch eventually decongested, we observed connections landing on one pod and piling up: One can observe that this is not many connections, only on the order of hundreds. On the client side we observed write requests began to taper off around the time of the congestion event, but even after relieved of congestion on the switch, write requests were near zero except for around 11:55a when we observed a brief respite along with one: ``` rpc error: code = Unavailable desc = transport is closing ``` error log captured from each client. The clients backoff their gRPC requests exponentially, however we only observed a single retry attempt over this 40 minute outage in our logs from each client, implying that the RPC itself on each client was somehow blocked and timing out and not exceeding context deadlines. Also, grpc requests tapered, declined, and recovered in a similar fashion based on logs from our nginx-ingress controller. The result of all these blocked RPCs is a build of messages on all the clients until we eventually deleted the grpc-go pods. At around 12:24pm we performed a rolling restart on all the pods running the grpc-go application containers, and as observed in the charts above, stale connections were closed, subsequently rebalancing more evenly, writes resumed successfully, and messages piled up on the clients flushed themselves immediately after being written upstream Unfortunately I do not have a pprof of all the go clients and servers during this outage. And although I've only observed this once and cannot reproduce it, this is a critical path and will raise alarms where I work if this is not resolved. ### What did you expect to see? I expected to see connections balanced evenly across gRPC pods and for the pods to not become unresponsive due to a small network switch congestion blip. In the case of the pods becoming unresponsive, we would normally expect to see gRPC failures exponentially backing off in our error logs, but this too did not occur. ### What did you see instead? Instead, I observed one pod accumulate all the connections after the congestion event and the gRPC pods become unresponsive. ### Addendum I'm anticipating someone to tell me to just upgrade to a newer version of grpc on all my clients and servers. Although it can be done, it is somewhat of a non-trivial task given how complex my organization is, and I am more interested in understanding how this can happen while noting that we've been using this particular version of the grpc-go libaries for nearly a year without having to upgrade. It might also be that we have a silent application bug in our client or server code whereby a goroutine handling the RPC blocks thus blocking subsequent RPCs. There could also be an issue with the nginx ingress controller similar to what is noted [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/issues/4054) and already resolved. But within the scope of this repository, I would like to rule out any possible issues with the grpc-go library particularly regarding sensitivity to Layer-3 network congestion that could affect the state of already established Layer-4 connections from grpc-go clients to grpc-go servers.

items.title: client: reset backoff to 0 after a connection is established
Reset backoff when interface goes up (or whenever application requests it)

labels.name: Type: Feature
labels.description: New features or improvements in behavior

items.body:
It would be great if GRPC would attempt to reconnect immediately after an interface goes up, for example when laptop connects to WiFi network. Instead of single reconnect attempt, it would be better to reset the exponential backoff, triggering a sequence of exponentially spaced retries, because interfaces can take a little while to actually start working after they report being up.

Perhaps this could be implemented as a single method (ResetBackoff? ReconnectNow?) on ClientConn that would allow applications to reset backoff at any moment. Applications could then choose their own reconnect events, for example when the app has an out of band information about server availability (a realistic scenario in my app). Interface monitoring could then be implemented on top of that, perhaps as a connection option.

Current workaround is to Close() the connection and recreate it at the cost of some application complexity. This involves reliably tracking health of the connection to avoid closing healthy connections, which AFAIK cannot be done in a simple way either. Another workaround is to set very short maximum backoff interval and supply dialer that implements custom backoff strategy on its own.

items.title: internal: refactor transport to single retry mechanism
items.body:
Previously, the transport was able to reset via the retry loop,
or via the event closures calling resetTransport. This meant
a very large amount of synchronization was necessary: one
reset meant the other had to not reset; state had to be kept
at the addrconn; and very subtle interactions were hard to
reason about.

This change removes the ability for event closures to directly
reset the transport. Instead, they signal to to the retry
loop about the event, and the retry loop is always the single
place that retries occur.

This also allows us to refactor the address switching logic
into a much simpler for loop inside the retry loop instead of
using addrConn state to keep track of an index.
